summary: Updates the eligibility rules for volunteering for the IETF Nominating Committee, in light of the fully online meetings of 2020 and 2021. It adjusts how meeting participation counts toward eligibility compared with RFC 8713.

plainLanguage.summary: The IETF Nominating Committee is a group of volunteers that puts forward candidates for the Internet's leadership positions, and the members are picked at random from everyone who qualifies. This document defines who qualifies. There are three ways in: turning up at three of the last five meetings, in person or online; having chaired a working group in the last three years; or having written at least two IETF documents in the last five years. Any one of the three is enough.

subtitle: The three ways to qualify for the IETF Nominating Committee, and why online attendance now counts.

tldr.problem: The IETF Nominating Committee picks candidates for several leadership positions, and it draws its members at random from a pool of volunteers. The old rule for joining that pool required attending three of the previous five meetings in person, which excluded people who take part remotely.
tldr.mechanism: The document replaces that rule with three alternative paths: attending three of the last five IETF meetings, in person or online; having served as a working group chair or secretary in the past three years; or being a listed author or editor of at least two IETF Stream RFCs in the past five years.
tldr.outcome: One of the three paths is enough, unless the person is disqualified for other reasons. The document updates RFC 8713, whose Section 4.14 holds the eligibility rules, and obsoletes RFC 8788 and RFC 8989.

today: RFC 9389 is a Best Current Practice published in April 2023. It updates RFC 8713, whose Section 4.14 holds the eligibility rules, and obsoletes RFC 8989 and RFC 8788. The attendance criteria it defines replaced the first two paragraphs of that section 4.14, and the rest of RFC 8713 is unchanged.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 8713 defines the process for selecting the Internet Architecture Board, the Internet Engineering Steering Group, the IETF Trust and the IETF LLC directors. A key actor in that process is the Nominating Committee, which nominates a single candidate for each open position; the nominations are then confirmed by other bodies.

NomCom voting members are selected at random from a pool of volunteers who meet certain eligibility requirements, so it matters that the people in that pool are IETF participants likely to know how the IETF works. There are also restrictions so that no more than two volunteers with the same primary affiliation are chosen.

Section 4.14 of RFC 8713 required volunteers to have attended three of the previous five meetings, which in practice meant collecting a registration badge at an in-person meeting. In 2020 and 2021 the IETF held six consecutive fully online plenary meetings, which pushed remote meeting technology and procedure forward quickly, and RFC 8989 ran an experiment that counted logging in to at least one session of a fully online meeting towards the requirement. RFC 8989 also created two other tracks to eligibility: serving as a working group chair or secretary in the past three years, and being an author or editor of an IETF Stream RFC in the past five years, which includes Internet-Drafts in the RFC Editor queue.

This document sets out the principles behind the eligibility rules and recommends how the attendance-based qualification should work. It replaces the attendance criteria in the first two paragraphs of Section 4.14 of RFC 8713 with the criteria of RFC 8989, and it obsoletes RFC 8989 to make clear that the document has been superseded. All other text in RFC 8713, including the other paragraphs of Section 4.14, remains unchanged. It also formally obsoletes RFC 8788, which set up procedures for the 2020-2021 NomCom.
sections.plainLanguage: The Nominating Committee puts forward candidates for the IETF's leadership positions, and its own members are picked at random from a pool of volunteers. The old rule for joining that pool was to attend three of the last five meetings in person, which was hard for people who take part remotely. This document sets the rule from first principles, and takes over the two extra routes that were tried out during the online meetings of 2020 and 2021.

sections.title: NomCom Principles
sections.content:
The NomCom is meant to be made up of randomly selected members of the community. For many years, in-person attendance was a reasonable proxy for the commitment that comes with being a member: two days of travel and an attendance fee are a relatively large outlay of time and money, and being in the room was thought to increase personal familiarity with candidates and with the spirit of the IETF, although no mechanism ensures any interaction.

A basic principle of the IETF is that the community should govern itself, so volunteers must show a demonstrated commitment to the IETF. Limiting the number of volunteers sponsored by any one organisation avoids the potential for mischief that disrupts IETF operations or works against the interests of the community as a whole.

A requirement for in-person attendance has always excluded some people from qualifying. As attitudes to business travel change and remote meeting technology improves, many long-standing community members are choosing to take part remotely, for cost or personal reasons, and the NomCom has completed two cycles using entirely online tools. Expanding the attendance requirement to include remote attendance lowers the barrier to entry: because the IETF has historically provided a fee-free remote participation option, the only investment required is to log on once per meeting at a specific time, sometimes at a locally inconvenient hour. The document does not formally require the NomCom to function entirely remotely, but including remote-only attendees in the pool is likely to make a remote component necessary in practice. Finally, overly restrictive criteria work against getting a broad talent pool.
sections.plainLanguage: The committee is meant to be a random cross-section of the community, and in-person attendance was used as a stand-in for commitment. That costs money and time, it keeps some committed people out, and it narrows the pool of candidates. Remote attendance is now cheap enough, and the IETF has long offered a free way to take part online, so the document treats logging in as attendance.

sections.title: The Three Paths to Eligibility
sections.content:
The text below replaces the first two paragraphs of Section 4.14 of RFC 8713. Members of the IETF community must satisfy the conditions in one of three paths in order to volunteer, and any one of the paths is sufficient, unless the person is otherwise disqualified under Section 4.15 of RFC 8713.

  • Path 1: the person has registered for and attended three out of the last five IETF meetings, either in person or online. In-person attendance is as determined by the record keeping of the Secretariat. Online attendance is based on being a registered person who logged in for at least one session of an IETF meeting.
  • Path 2: the person has been a Working Group Chair or Secretary within the three years prior to the day the call for NomCom volunteers is sent to the community.
  • Path 3: the person has been a listed author or editor on the front page of at least two IETF Stream RFCs within the last five years prior to the day the call for NomCom volunteers is sent to the community. An Internet-Draft that has been approved by the IESG and is in the RFC Editor queue counts the same as a published RFC, with the relevant date being the date the draft was added to the RFC Editor queue. The five-year timer runs back to the date five years before the call for NomCom volunteers is sent to the community.
sections.plainLanguage: You qualify if you have done any one of three things: attended three of the last five meetings, in person or online; chaired or been secretary of a working group in the last three years; or been listed as an author or editor on at least two IETF documents in the last five years. A document that is approved and waiting in the RFC Editor queue counts, dated from when it entered the queue.

sections.title: The Risk of NomCom Capture
sections.content:
The most potent threat associated with NomCom eligibility is that an organisation, or a group of coordinating organisations, tries to obtain a majority of the NomCom positions in order to select an IETF leadership that supports an agenda which is self-serving and against the interests of the community as a whole. RFC 8713 lets the NomCom Chair decide the voting requirement, so a simple majority may not be enough, but seven of ten forms a quorum, so at worst seven NomCom members working together can impose their will.

Whatever the merits of admitting remote attendees, it lowers the minimum cost of producing an eligible volunteer from three in-person trips of around five days each over at least eight months, to no financial cost and the time needed to log in three times over at least eight months. Some organisations might not be deterred in either case, while others might.

A large number of legitimate volunteers makes it hard to control a majority of the seats, and the document works out the arithmetic in its appendix. To have even a 50% chance of controlling six or more positions, an attacker needs roughly 60% of the volunteer pool: if there are 300 legitimate volunteers, an attacker must produce 365 to exceed a 50% chance of capture. A sudden surge in the number of volunteers, particularly of people nobody recognises as part of the community, is an early warning sign of an attempt at capture, and anyone with concerns about the integrity of the process should bring them to the IESG to investigate. The confirming bodies can then take action to invalidate candidates, as defined in Section 3.7.3 of RFC 8713. Loosening the criteria lowers the cost of producing eligible volunteers, but it also raises the number of legitimate volunteers, which makes an attack harder.

The two-per-organisation limit of Section 4.17 of RFC 8713 complicates such an attack. To get round it, an organisation would have to coordinate with at least two like-minded organisations, incentivise members of other organisations, or propose candidates with false affiliations. The IETF does not routinely confirm affiliation, but an investigation could eliminate volunteers who misrepresented it, and publishing the list of volunteers and their affiliations gives the community a chance to review such claims. Assuming 300 legitimate volunteers, all from different organisations, three conspiring organisations would need 771 volunteers, 257 per organisation, for a 50% chance of capture. Finally, attending three meetings takes at least eight months of waiting, so an attack needs a surge over the course of a year, which might trigger a community challenge or a leadership investigation, and the leadership would then have months to adjust policy before the NomCom cycle begins.
sections.plainLanguage: The main danger is that one organisation, or a few acting together, tries to fill enough seats to pick a leadership that serves its own interests. The document argues that the rules still hold up: the pool has to be large for that to work, a sudden flood of unfamiliar volunteers is a warning sign, and there are limits on how many people one organisation may sponsor. The appendix works out the numbers.

sections.title: Disruptive Candidates and Other Remedies
sections.content:
Counting remote participation towards eligibility allows a single individual to mount an attack that previously required coordination. By registering for remote attendance at IETF meetings under a number of different identities over a year, an individual can make each of those identities eligible, and then serve under whichever one is selected. Once selected, such an individual could seek to disrupt the process or prevent the timely conclusion of its work; less severely, an attacker could simply improve their chances of being selected. This attack is much harder to detect or prevent than the equivalent attacks under the old rules, because it needs no coordination among several attendees, and the lower cost of remote participation makes it more feasible. The attacker cannot be sure of fee waivers for all the different identities, but that is the only remaining obstacle.

The voting member recall procedure in Section 5.7 of RFC 8713 exists to allow the removal and replacement of disruptive figures. Further changes to the process are beyond the scope of this document, but the document points to two more that could help. A challenge process against volunteers with a suspicious reported affiliation, or that might be aliases of a single volunteer, could trigger an investigation. And the challenge to the random selection described in Section 4.17 of RFC 8713 could explicitly include appeals against the data used to qualify the volunteer, rather than against the randomisation process itself.
sections.plainLanguage: One person can now use several identities to get several entries into the pool and then serve under whichever one is drawn, and that is harder to spot than the old attacks, which needed several people to work together. The answer the document gives is the existing recall procedure, plus the idea of letting anyone challenge the data behind a volunteer's eligibility rather than only the draw itself.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: This document has no IANA actions. It registers no names, numbers or protocol parameters, because it changes only the text of other documents: it updates RFC 8713 and obsoletes RFC 8989 and RFC 8788.
sections.plainLanguage: There is nothing to register with IANA here, because the document only changes the wording of other documents.
